title: Editorial: Wine needs new consumers. Now what?

The post Editorial: Wine needs new consumers. Now what? appeared first on winemag.
content:
Over the weekend, a group of perhaps a dozen adults gathered around a braai. Two-thirds were English-speaking, one-third Afrikaans-speaking – an unusual enough combination to prompt a conversation about language. Why, someone asked, was I not fluent in Afrikaans despite having studied at Stellenbosch University? My response was that, at least, I had Afrikaans friends. What struck me afterwards was that I couldn’t say the same about having black friends.

The global wine industry faces a challenge that is now impossible to look past: consumers are drinking less.

There is less agreement about why. Demographic change, health concerns, economic pressure and competition from other alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages are all offered as explanations. The causes matter, but perhaps less than the consequence. Wine has a demand problem, and the old growth models are no longer available to solve it.

That ought to prompt a more radical question than how we tell wine’s story: What if the industry needs to change the way wine is experienced, discovered and discussed?

It dawned on me that a key part of the problem is not poor communication of a compelling consumer promise, but a lack of relevance at a more fundamental level. I wrote about this earlier this year, arguing that wine’s problem isn’t a shortage of stories but a shortage of reasons for people to care. That remains my view. The harder question is what needs to change.

Technology: opportunity or trivialisation?

The danger is that technology makes wine more accessible while making it more trivial. Wine has enthusiastically embraced digital marketing while remaining remarkably attached to analogue ways of helping people choose what to drink.

A consumer still encounters a shelf containing dozens of bottles, differentiated by labels, regions, varieties, vintages and producer names. The information required to make a confident choice can be considerable.

Technology can make this easier. AI, for example, could become a useful wine intermediary – not a robot sommelier making grandiose pronouncements, but a tool that translates expertise into the questions ordinary drinkers actually ask.

Is this dry? Full-bodied? Fresh and linear or soft and smooth-textured? What should I eat with it? Is there something similar but cheaper? If I liked this bottle, what else might I enjoy? Is this a wine to drink tonight or keep for five years?

These are not intellectually inferior questions. They are the questions that get wine into people’s glasses.

The opportunity, then, is not to use technology to produce more wine content. There is already plenty of that. It is to reduce the effort required to participate in wine. We don’t need an infinite number of tasting notes generated by machines – God forbid, humans are already adequate at that. We need better ways of connecting a particular person with a particular wine.

But there is a caution. Personalisation can easily become another form of narrowing, giving us more of what we already like while reducing the chance of encountering something unexpected. At the same time, digital wine culture has its own cliques, and the people within them can end up deciding what is fashionable, desirable or worth talking about. Technology may therefore democratise access to wine while creating new forms of gatekeeping around taste.

Its more interesting role would be to do the opposite: broaden discovery, expose people to wines and ideas beyond the circles they already inhabit, and make it easier for new voices to influence what wine becomes.

Who gets to define wine?

I am 55, white, male and based in Cape Town. I have spent more than two decades working professionally in wine. I know a great deal about the subject and have accumulated plenty of assumptions about what matters in wine, how it should be discussed and what constitutes expertise.

But the episode around the braai left me wondering how well equipped I am to understand what might make wine relevant to people whose lives and experiences have historically had so little meaningful contact with it. If my own social world can remain so racially circumscribed after 55 years in South Africa, perhaps the wine industry should be less surprised that its attempts to connect with black consumers so often feel superficial.

My experience has value. But it does not make me the ideal interlocutor with every future wine consumer. This is particularly pertinent when we talk about South Africa’s emerging Black middle class. The answer isn’t simply to market wine more effectively to Black consumers. Nor is it to recruit a handful of Black personalities as ambassadors while leaving the underlying culture untouched.

If new consumers are to become part of wine’s future, they need a genuine role in shaping it. That means more Black winemakers, yes, but also more Black retailers, sommeliers, marketers, educators, writers and entrepreneurs with the power to influence the category. It means allowing different social occasions, tastes and cultural references to shape how wine is presented and consumed.

And it means those of us who have traditionally occupied positions of authority accepting that relevance may involve giving up some control over the conversation. That isn’t a threat to expertise. It is a test of whether expertise can adapt.

The wine industry sometimes treats the new consumer as though they are waiting to be persuaded to appreciate what we already appreciate. That is the wrong starting point.

The more productive question is: what might wine become when people who have historically been outside its cultural centre start influencing it?

The answer should not be “wine dumbed down”. Nor should it be “wine as we know it, but with younger faces”. Nor should it be wine reinvented so completely that it loses any connection with its history.

The industry should retain the things that make wine worth caring about – place, craft, history, agriculture, diversity and pleasure – while becoming much less prescriptive about how consumers encounter them.

That may mean different formats, occasions, price points, voices and ways of talking about taste. It may mean wine appearing in spaces where it has not traditionally appeared, alongside food, music and culture without demanding that everyone first learn its vocabulary. One of the reasons I detest “minerality” as a descriptor is that it illustrates the problem perfectly: what insiders regard as useful shorthand can sound like nonsense to everyone else.

And it may mean accepting that some of the things enthusiasts consider important simply aren’t important to everyone else. That is not necessarily decline. It may be democratisation.

As we know all too well, vineyards are being pulled out and production is contracting. The difficult work now is not managing abundance but rebuilding demand. We cannot assume that the next generation will inherit wine culture simply because previous generations did. They have more choices, different media habits and different relationships with authority. They also have no obligation to preserve our hierarchies.

So what would I suggest? Use technology to make wine easier to discover and understand, without reducing it to disposable content. Communicate in ways that begin with consumers’ lives rather than wine’s internal vocabulary. Create more opportunities for participation rather than simply more opportunities to consume marketing. And, above all, broaden who gets to shape the category.

For someone like me, there is a final responsibility: to remain useful without assuming that I must remain central. That may be the hardest adjustment of all.

title: Recipe: Tofu, tat soi and shimeji mushroom stir-fry
summary:
Delicious served with steamed rice. Serves 4 Ingredients: 3 tbsp (45ml) sunflower oil 400g tofu, drained and patted dry with absorbent paper 60g shimeji mushrooms, cleaned ¼ cup (60ml) ginger, finely chopped 2 tsp (10ml) sesame seed oil 3 tbsp (45ml) soy sauce 3 tbsp (45ml) sweet chilli sauce squeeze of lemon 200g tat soi, […]

The post Recipe: Tofu, tat soi and shimeji mushroom stir-fry appeared first on winemag.
content:
Serve with Kruger Family Wines Old Vines Cinsault 2017.

Delicious served with steamed rice.

Serves 4

Ingredients:
3 tbsp (45ml) sunflower oil
400g tofu, drained and patted dry with absorbent paper
60g shimeji mushrooms, cleaned
¼ cup (60ml) ginger, finely chopped
2 tsp (10ml) sesame seed oil
3 tbsp (45ml) soy sauce
3 tbsp (45ml) sweet chilli sauce
squeeze of lemon
200g tat soi, washed
15g coriander, chopped
steamed basmati rice, to serve

Method:
Cube tofu into bite size portions and set aside.

Heat sunflower oil in a non-stick pan until hot and gently shallow-fry tofu until golden brown and crispy. Add mushrooms and ginger and stir-fry for further five  minutes. Add sesame oil, soy sauce, sweet chilli sauce and a squeeze of lemon.

Toss in tat soi and remove pan from heat allowing the leaves to wilt. Check seasoning.

Serve with steamed basmati rice and fresh coriander.

Wine pairing:
Light-bodied reds you can chill will work with this dish – think Pinot Noir or new-wave Cinsault.

  • Recipe supplied by Source Food – a Cape Town-based food agency that specializes in experiential marketing. They will create a recipe or meal to communicate your brand’s message.

title: Tim James: Growing older, drinking differently
summary:
We know about old vines and old wines – and their age makes a difference. But what about old wine-drinkers? Does age bring changes, for better or worse, in taste-experiences and preferences? It was a question that the American winewriter and -importer Terry Theise raised in the latest issue of World of Fine Wine, prompted […]

The post Tim James: Growing older, drinking differently appeared first on winemag.
content:
We know about old vines and old wines – and their age makes a difference. But what about old wine-drinkers? Does age bring changes, for better or worse, in taste-experiences and preferences? It was a question that the American winewriter and -importer Terry Theise raised in the latest issue of World of Fine Wine, prompted by his own experience (he didn’t announce it there, but tells me he’s 73). This led to wondering about physical changes that might prompt changes in taste: a supposed reduction in acuity, for example; and he mentioned the presumably hormonal changes in older women – but I guess those in men might also be expected to have consequences.

Theise was surprised, however, to find that most of the small handful of wine-professional friends and colleagues he consulted reported no significant patterns of change in their wine-tastes.

I too am surprised. Easy continuity is not my own experience, whatever the causes of my shifts. Given that I’ve noticeably changed my tastes in various aesthetic areas that are important to me, why not my wine-drinking? These days I seldom read novels, for example, and novel-reading was a defining factor of my life for decades, professional and personal. Overall I now read less than I used to, and it’s usually re-reading rather than anything new, and more often than not it’s non-fiction. My musical tastes have shifted too: it’s still all “classical”, but I can’t easily recall how much I used to love Italian opera (mostly unspeakably silly stuff, I now think, though often kitschly beautiful); and generally I have moved in both temporal directions away from the lushness of nineteenth-century Romanticism.

So, again, why not changes in my tastes in wine as I’ve got older? I’m now 71, having begun a more-or-less serious relationship with wine only in my latter 30s. I don’t think these changes are all obviously ascribable to bodily changes any more than are my shifts in musical and literary tastes … but, yes, maybe some. I have certainly had a general reduction in my taste for sweet foods and drinks in the last decade or two, and that is plausibly related to bodily changes. So my beloved older-style German rieslings often seem too sweet and I would reluctantly admit to, on the whole, preferring drier ones.

When acidity loses its appeal

This is something that Terry Theise strongly notices too. Interestingly (given the high acidity in the best of those sweet rieslings) he also notes a change that he says is more age-typical: a resistance to very high acidity in wines, a character he used to relish. I hadn’t thought of that for myself, but I think it applies. It would help explain why at tastings I seem to object more than my younger colleagues to the “hipster” style of lowish-alcohol, ultra-fresh wines, both white and red, and tend to find them unbalanced and even aggressive in their acidity.

Taking this further, I wonder if this also accounts for my mild turn in the last decade or so away from the red burgundies and local pinot noirs that I previously enjoyed so much more. I’ve returned more , in fact, to an earlier love: cabernet sauvignon-based blends – especially from Bordeaux, especially the dark-fruited, savoury, tannic and “sinister” ones that hark back to pre-1982 times (but seldom South African examples, which I can admire theoretically occasionally, but seldom love, because they are that bit too sunny and friendly, even when not too ripe and powerful). Tannin, then, suits me now more than acidity, it seems.

The pleasures of caring less

As to a decline in acuity – well, I don’t think I’ve ever been acute as a taster, nor have I aspired to become more so, though I realise that this might seem odd for someone who, for example, tasted and rated for the annual Platter’s Guide for two decades. Aiming for the finest, geekiest discrimination has never interested me nearly as much as other aspects of wine (social, historical, cultural, agricultural) – even less now. Decades back, I got through giving up smoking cigarettes without being aware that it made much difference to my palate. Having now joyfully abandoned writing more than the briefest of tasting notes has been an enormous liberation. (I can’t say I frequently read others’ notes either.) It’s very possible that this liberation has itself positively affected the way I enjoy wine in all circumstances: an aura of anxiousness – coming from a sense of responsibility and of my likely inadequacy – doesn’t cloud the pleasure.

There’s much less detail that I’m concerned with these days, Possibly that marks a decline. But I read, just this morning over my toast and marmalade, this apposite line from Montaigne about the comfort he finds in old age, in an essay entitled “All things have their season”:  “that it deadens in me many desires and cares by which life is troubled”, including “care for knowledge”. There’s so much about the vast world of wine that I no longer feel curious about, as I did when I would read the Oxford Companion to Wine cover to cover. That reduction in interest is more of an admission, I suppose, than a boast.

Some changes in my tastes – as reflected in my drinking practices – are clearly not so much so much about ageing as about my growing older in a particular place and time. I’ve had a good few decades chronicling – and drinking – the Cape wine revolution. South African fine white wine is, widely, a miraculously delicate, not to mention delicious, expression of its origins. In response, I now drink nearly as much white wine as red, and that’s a notable shift. As all wine gets more expensive, local and foreign, and I don’t get richer, it suits me well to buy and drink for my pleasure lots of Cape white, and little foreign white apart from sherry and what good German riesling I can afford.

As for the local reds, I prefer the Rhône-style ones, based on syrah or grenache – the whole range of them, including the lighter, fresher ones (but not too light) with no new oak. There’s another change, I think: I now get more pleasure than before from comparatively simple, fairly young wines. I don’t think I’d even want to drink only fine, mature, serious wines, even as an aspiration. Perhaps it’s a sign of greater tolerance.

Something else. I’ve always had a particular passion for fortified wine: sherry, port, madeira. But now, along with drinking some younger, lighter wines, I also go to the opposite extreme and drink a good amount of brandy. I seem to like that kick at the end of the day. My total alcohol consumption has probably declined a little in the last decade, but the proportion of the alcohol intake provided by brandy has increased.

That’s a change in my drinking habits that I am at a total loss to explain. The great revolutionary Leon Trotsky once said that “’Old age is the most unexpected of all things that can happen to a man.” That’s true, I think, and many of the details of the process are just as surprising.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

title: Malu Lambert: The Foundry – 25 Years of Rhône in the Cape
summary:
There is no better way to explore Rhône varieties in South Africa than through The Foundry’s wines, which set a benchmark for a distinctly Cape interpretation. “The Foundry is 25-years-old this year,” says Chris Williams addressing trade and media on the rooftop of the Melting Pot restaurant. The day is vibrantly hot, the surrounding technicolor […]

The post Malu Lambert: The Foundry – 25 Years of Rhône in the Cape appeared first on winemag.
content:
There is no better way to explore Rhône varieties in South Africa than through The Foundry’s wines, which set a benchmark for a distinctly Cape interpretation.

Chris Williams of The Foundry.

“The Foundry is 25-years-old this year,” says Chris Williams addressing trade and media on the rooftop of the Melting Pot restaurant. The day is vibrantly hot, the surrounding technicolor buildings of De Waterkant seem to pulse in its brightness. It’s the new vintage-release and the label’s cold viognier is the perfect counterpoint to the weather.

The Foundry “was born very much out of the impact that the Rhône made on me as a young winemaker travelling in 1994”. Established in an old shed at Joostenberg while Williams was at Meerlust, he left in 2020 to focus on the brand full-time.

“It looks like it was a plan,” he says of the five Rhône-style wines we are about to taste. “It wasn’t. The first vintage [2001] was a mishmash of varieties, but the syrah really stood out.” In 2004, he started co-fermenting syrah with viognier. “I liked the gloss, but not the sweetness and overt florals.” Instead, viognier became The Foundry’s second wine and its first white.

“The range evolved organically.” Part of this is the Cape’s suitability. “There are a lot of similarities with the Rhône,” he says, citing granite soils, a Mediterranean climate, windy summers and cold, wet winters. Crucially, says Williams, “they retain their flavour and acidity.”

White masquerading as red

The Viognier 2024 comes from a vineyard six kilometres from False Bay. At 13 per cent alcohol, it is linear, floral and restrained, with less opulence than typical examples. It’s the only wine made entirely in oak: “Terracotta took away too much of the variety’s perfume.”

We move on to the Grenache Blanc 2022 (Williams says it benefits from bottle age). He points out that few places in the world produce a single varietal. “It’s a very Cape style of wine.” By contrast, some examples he’s tasted in southern France and Spain are “actually quite dull”, where the grape is often used for volume and alcohol.

The grapes come primarily from his own Voor-Paardeberg vineyard with the rest from neighbouring grower Willie Mostert. Williams south-facing block ripens about a week later than Mostert’s sunnier, east-facing vineyard. Each vineyard is split into three cuvées: barrel, stainless steel and terracotta. “What makes it so interesting, both red and white, is the mouthfeel,” he posits. “You get this textural pithiness on the mid-palate after the fruit explosion on entry.”

That component is what draws him to the whites. “They’re thick-skinned because they’ve evolved to deal with the harsh climate of the southern Rhône.” The Foundry whites all have varying degrees of grip balanced by fruit and fresh acidity.

With the Roussanne 2024 now in glass, he points out its gold colour, due to its phenolic character. “I’m careful to balance the natural tannin with roussanne’s generous fruit.” Its skin-to-juice ratio yields just 500 litres per tonne from his Voor-Paardeberg vineyard. “Squish a grape and basically a blob of pulp with four seeds comes out.”

The 2024 is perfumed with incense, turmeric, and Chinese five-spice, offset by savouriness and lemony acidity. Fermented equally in terracotta and barrel, it needs oxygen “to really unlock these exotic flavours”.

“I’ve referred to it, usually after a bottle or two, as red wine in drag.” Roussanne, he adds, has incredible ageing potential, noting that his first vintage was 2010 and “that wine is only now fully mature”. One of his favourite wines, he says, is Château de Beaucastel’s Roussanne Vieilles Vignes, which “is just indestructible”.

Fresh and focused reds

“The inclusion of whole bunch is dependent on the stems,” says Williams, answering a question about the Grenache Noir 2022. “Too green, the wine becomes overtly grassy. Too brown you get a lignified character.”

Heady with roses, the grenache “comes across seductively on the nose, but the palate reminds you that it’s a wine of substance, with this core of tannin.” The key, he says, is picking before overripeness; grenache’s tendency to overcrop and ripen unevenly makes yield and canopy management crucial.

“I don’t like a lot of alcohol; it takes away from the typicity. Freshness and brightness are what I look for.”

The final wine is the Syrah 2022, from Williams’s own Voor-Paardeberg vineyard, planted in 2000. “I like to think of this wine as straddling a tightrope: plenty of freshness, no excess ripeness, quite lithe and muscular. That’s the style the vineyard lends itself to.”

Viognier may not have worked as a blending partner, but Williams has found success with roussanne, which makes up six per cent of the wine. “I discovered too late in life that in Hermitage a lot of growers harvest a bit of roussanne with their syrah.” Unlike viognier, it brings no overt sweetness or perfume, instead it tempers the syrah’s rusticity, glossing its tannins and adding brightness.

While Williams’s unintentional 25-year experiment makes a compelling case for Rhône varieties in the Cape, a conversation with viticulturist Etienne Terblanche after the tasting adds some perspective.

Grenache says Terblanche is the clearest success story. Against the backdrop of an overall decline in vineyard area, grenache noir has grown from around 50 ha in the early 2000s to some 570–580 ha today, while grenache blanc has increased from roughly 20 ha to 170 ha.

Varieties such as marsanne and roussanne grew from a low base but have largely stabilised over the past decade, while viognier, once planted to around 900–1,000 ha, has since roughly halved.

Mourvèdre is also waning. Terblanche believes commercial viability is part of the equation: varieties such as grenache have enough identity to stand alone, while lesser-known grapes primarily associated with blends can be difficult to communicate and sell. Nor he says are these varieties necessarily a simple answer to climate change. While adapted to warm, dry conditions and useful for increasing varietal diversity, many Rhône whites are naturally more about texture than crisp acidity.

The vineyards need to mature too, young plantings of big-berried varieties such as grenache, carignan and cinsault can take time to come into their own.

What do the next 25 years hold for these grapes? While we wait, to borrow from Williams’s favourite writer, Henry David Thoreau: “Live in each season as it passes; breathe the air, drink the drink, taste the fruit…”.

  • Malu Lambert is a freelance wine journalist and wine judge who has written for numerous local and international titles. She is a WSET Diploma alum and won the title of Louis Roederer Emerging Wine Writer of the Year 2019, among many other accolades. She sits on various tasting panels and has judged in competitions abroad. Follow her on X: @MaluLambert

title: Greg Sherwood MW: Wine, giving and the Pebbles Project
summary:
Over the years, I have read a lot of periodical analyses and critiques about how the South African wine industry is not doing enough when it comes to helping the disadvantaged communities it relies so heavily upon to operate as a successful industry. Some of it may be fact, some of it fiction, but whenever […]

The post Greg Sherwood MW: Wine, giving and the Pebbles Project appeared first on winemag.
content:
Over the years, I have read a lot of periodical analyses and critiques about how the South African wine industry is not doing enough when it comes to helping the disadvantaged communities it relies so heavily upon to operate as a successful industry. Some of it may be fact, some of it fiction, but whenever I am spending longer periods of time in the Cape winelands, I am always curious and enquiring as to what specific projects are successfully operating in the winelands and making a real impact on real peoples’ lives.

On my recent trip to the Cape, I managed to not only spend a week in Stellenbosch judging but also spent an extended time in both Franschhoek and Hemel-en-Aarde. Knowing full well that my time in and around Hermanus would be pulled in a number of directions, I contacted Carolyn Martin of Creation and enquired if there would be any opportunity to do a charity wine dinner for consumers to help raise funds for a local charity.

Carolyn, being the indomitable force that she is, thought it would be a great idea to get some of the local wineries involved in a fine wine dinner to help raise funds for their local branch of Pebbles Project, a charity I had encountered many times before through the very generous fundraising work of ex-Mullineux Wines shareholder Keith Prothero in London, as well as during my time as the Cape Wine Auction’s UK Charity Ambassador, Pebbles Project being a significant beneficiary of the funds raised annually.

Wine farms and social impact

To be honest, I primarily thought that the Pebbles Project was mostly active in and around Stellenbosch but was pleasantly surprised to see how its incredible network had grown to cover great swathes of the Cape’s winelands. The Pebbles Project is a South African non-profit founded in 2004 that works to improve the lives of children and families in the country’s agricultural communities, many of whom are the sons, daughters, and relatives of wine farm workers.

Operating across Somerset West, Stellenbosch, Paarl, Wellington, Citrusdal, and the Hemel-en-Aarde region near Hermanus, Pebbles, as I learnt, currently supports over 1,400 children between the ages of 0 and 18, alongside their families. Its work follows a five-pillar approach covering education, health, nutrition, community development, and child protection through social work programmes, addressing challenges such as poverty, alcohol abuse, and limited access to basic services that are common in farming communities.

As it turns out, one of the organisation’s most notable initiatives happens to be in the Hemel-en-Aarde outside Hermanus. In 2015, Carolyn Martin, co-owner of Creation Wines, approached the Pebbles Project to develop educational facilities for farming families in the Valley.  A local farm owner made available a 10-hectare piece of land, and seed funding from the Cape Wine Auction Trust enabled the opening of an Early Childhood Development and After-School Club centre in 2016. 

The project has since grown substantially: a Rotary Global grant in 2019 funded two additional classrooms, and by 2020 the centre had grown from 62 to 113 learners. Carolyn then explained that when a neighbouring government school closed in 2019 leaving 34 farm children without placements, Pebbles partnered with several donors to open the Pebbles Academy, accommodating learners from Grade 1 to 9. A skills development centre was later added, converting an old onion shed into a facility for 20 young adult learners, in partnership with the Hermanus Rotary Club and international donors.

This is exactly the kind of model that illustrates the strength of cooperation between local wineries and the Pebbles Project, with wine estates providing land, funding, and advocacy, while Pebbles delivers the on-the-ground infrastructure and expertise, together transforming opportunities for generations of farming families. It is projects like this and many others that I believe are simply not talked about enough, with even affluent locals often unaware of the tireless work going on in the background and the ongoing funding demands.

So, on a crisp but very muddy Friday morning, after a long-awaited overnight Walker Bay downpour, I set off with Carolyn to visit the Pebbles Academy in the Valley. Carolyn said we would need at least an hour or so on site, which initially seemed quite long to me. But it was only when I got to the Pebbles Academy and saw its true extent, that I realised what a large and groundbreaking undertaking it really was.

As things turned out, we were there a lot longer than an hour and speaking to all the incredible teachers and children was truly inspiring. The profound effect the opportunities offered by the Academy are having on the children was clear to see. Young lives being changed, improved and enhanced through educational opportunities, a healthy routine and an all-important ‘safe space’ respite away from some of the starker realities of a hard rural upbringing.

A dinner that raised more than R50,000

Heading to the sell-out wine tasting dinner in Hermanus that evening at the Fisherman’s Cottage restaurant, which I was presenting alongside Cape Wine Master Liezl Richards, took on a whole new significance. Beyond the interest and consumer support drummed up by Carolyn Martin, a special mention needs to go to the incredibly generous wineries that provided some sensational wines on the night: Creation, Newton Johnson, Restless River, Crystallum and Thamnus.

Flight one featured four Chardonnays including Thamnus Chardonnay 2023, an embryonically youthful and vibrant wine with more opulent high-tone fruit notes of fresh green honeydew melon, green apple, white pear, and a stony mineral limestone complexity. This was served alongside the excellent Newton Johnson Family Vineyards Chardonnay 2024, sourced from multiple vineyards to reflect the estate in its entirety, showing pear, peach, citrus, and vanilla notes, the palate poised and elegant.

The second pairing featured another blockbuster duo, with Restless River’s incredible Ava Marie Chardonnay 2023 brimming with tension and struck flint minerality along side notes of lemon and herbs, lemon cordial and white peach notes that intermingled with the fabulous stony mineral nuances. This was served with Creation’s top white offering, the Art of Chardonnay 2024, a steely, crystalline expression with incredible tension and focus, wound spring energy and a lemon and lime persistence of note. 2024 is a seriously good vintage in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, despite being a very small harvest.

With three food courses appearing alongside the wine pairings, the first two reds were every bit as exciting as the Chardonnays. The Thamnus Pinot Noir 2022 was layered with sour red plum, black berry, curry leaf and bruised ripe strawberry fruits, the palate imparting a fullness and ripeness with a feel of density and dry extract. The Newton Johnson Family Vineyards Pinot Noir 2024 is also a serious vintage offering, rating an impressive 95/100 from Winemag’s editor, and showing lashings of strawberry, red and black cherry, pink musk and fynbos spice with a rich, succulent palate.

The final red pairing to round out the evening was the always impressive Crystallum Cuvee Cinema Pinot Noir 2024, shining bright with incredibly pure, finessed, supple red and black bramble berry fruits and a pinpoint focus on the palate, served alongside Creation’s beautiful Art of Pinot Noir 2024 flagship red. The aromatics showed incredible intensity with piercing notes of black cherry, black berry and wild strawberry, the palate fruit tempered by a fresh, pure stony minerality and a superb fine-grained texture.

A big thank you has to go to all the wonderful Hermanus residents who supported this Pebbles Project charity dinner so generously, with a notable R1,000 of every ticket sold going directly into the charity’s coffers. Adding to that the funds from two silent auctions of mixed wine rarity cases from the above wineries as well as a generous magnum of Pinot Noir donated by Anthony Hamilton Russell, the evening helped raise well over R50,000.

I cannot take any credit for the hard work in putting the whole evening together, merely for floating the original idea and letting other people run with it, but I was certainly very thankful to have had Carolyn and JC Martin’s generous time and energy as well as the able support of Liezl Richards CWM to help present all the wines on the night. As is so often the case, giving can be so much more rewarding than receiving.

If you would like to donate or assist The Pebbles Project in any way, they can be contacted at: www.pebblesproject.org

  • Greg Sherwood was born in Pretoria, South Africa, and as the son of a career diplomat, spent his first 21 years traveling the globe with his parents. With a Business Management and Marketing degree from Webster University, St. Louis, Missouri, USA, Sherwood began his working career as a commodity trader. In 2000, he decided to make more of a long-held interest in wine taking a position at Handford Wines in South Kensington, London, working his way up to the position of Senior Wine Buyer over 22 years. Sherwood currently consults to a number of top fine wine merchants in London while always keeping one eye firmly on the South African wine industry. He qualified as the 303rd Master of Wine in 2007.

title: Editorial: Wine needs new consumers. Now what?
summary:
Over the weekend, a group of perhaps a dozen adults gathered around a braai. Two-thirds were English-speaking, one-third Afrikaans-speaking – an unusual enough combination to prompt a conversation about language. Why, someone asked, was I not fluent in Afrikaans despite having studied at Stellenbosch University? My response was that, at least, I had Afrikaans friends. […]

The post Editorial: Wine needs new consumers. Now what? appeared first on winemag.
content:
Over the weekend, a group of perhaps a dozen adults gathered around a braai. Two-thirds were English-speaking, one-third Afrikaans-speaking – an unusual enough combination to prompt a conversation about language. Why, someone asked, was I not fluent in Afrikaans despite having studied at Stellenbosch University? My response was that, at least, I had Afrikaans friends. What struck me afterwards was that I couldn’t say the same about having black friends.

The global wine industry faces a challenge that is now impossible to look past: consumers are drinking less.

There is less agreement about why. Demographic change, health concerns, economic pressure and competition from other alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages are all offered as explanations. The causes matter, but perhaps less than the consequence. Wine has a demand problem, and the old growth models are no longer available to solve it.

That ought to prompt a more radical question than how we tell wine’s story: What if the industry needs to change the way wine is experienced, discovered and discussed?

It dawned on me that a key part of the problem is not poor communication of a compelling consumer promise, but a lack of relevance at a more fundamental level. I wrote about this earlier this year, arguing that wine’s problem isn’t a shortage of stories but a shortage of reasons for people to care. That remains my view. The harder question is what needs to change.

Technology: opportunity or trivialisation?

The danger is that technology makes wine more accessible while making it more trivial. Wine has enthusiastically embraced digital marketing while remaining remarkably attached to analogue ways of helping people choose what to drink.

A consumer still encounters a shelf containing dozens of bottles, differentiated by labels, regions, varieties, vintages and producer names. The information required to make a confident choice can be considerable.

Technology can make this easier. AI, for example, could become a useful wine intermediary – not a robot sommelier making grandiose pronouncements, but a tool that translates expertise into the questions ordinary drinkers actually ask.

Is this dry? Full-bodied? Fresh and linear or soft and smooth-textured? What should I eat with it? Is there something similar but cheaper? If I liked this bottle, what else might I enjoy? Is this a wine to drink tonight or keep for five years?

These are not intellectually inferior questions. They are the questions that get wine into people’s glasses.

The opportunity, then, is not to use technology to produce more wine content. There is already plenty of that. It is to reduce the effort required to participate in wine. We don’t need an infinite number of tasting notes generated by machines – God forbid, humans are already adequate at that. We need better ways of connecting a particular person with a particular wine.

But there is a caution. Personalisation can easily become another form of narrowing, giving us more of what we already like while reducing the chance of encountering something unexpected. At the same time, digital wine culture has its own cliques, and the people within them can end up deciding what is fashionable, desirable or worth talking about. Technology may therefore democratise access to wine while creating new forms of gatekeeping around taste.

Its more interesting role would be to do the opposite: broaden discovery, expose people to wines and ideas beyond the circles they already inhabit, and make it easier for new voices to influence what wine becomes.

Who gets to define wine?

I am 55, white, male and based in Cape Town. I have spent more than two decades working professionally in wine. I know a great deal about the subject and have accumulated plenty of assumptions about what matters in wine, how it should be discussed and what constitutes expertise.

But the episode around the braai left me wondering how well equipped I am to understand what might make wine relevant to people whose lives and experiences have historically had so little meaningful contact with it. If my own social world can remain so racially circumscribed after 55 years in South Africa, perhaps the wine industry should be less surprised that its attempts to connect with black consumers so often feel superficial.

My experience has value. But it does not make me the ideal interlocutor with every future wine consumer. This is particularly pertinent when we talk about South Africa’s emerging Black middle class. The answer isn’t simply to market wine more effectively to Black consumers. Nor is it to recruit a handful of Black personalities as ambassadors while leaving the underlying culture untouched.

If new consumers are to become part of wine’s future, they need a genuine role in shaping it. That means more Black winemakers, yes, but also more Black retailers, sommeliers, marketers, educators, writers and entrepreneurs with the power to influence the category. It means allowing different social occasions, tastes and cultural references to shape how wine is presented and consumed.

And it means those of us who have traditionally occupied positions of authority accepting that relevance may involve giving up some control over the conversation. That isn’t a threat to expertise. It is a test of whether expertise can adapt.

The wine industry sometimes treats the new consumer as though they are waiting to be persuaded to appreciate what we already appreciate. That is the wrong starting point.

The more productive question is: what might wine become when people who have historically been outside its cultural centre start influencing it?

The answer should not be “wine dumbed down”. Nor should it be “wine as we know it, but with younger faces”. Nor should it be wine reinvented so completely that it loses any connection with its history.

The industry should retain the things that make wine worth caring about – place, craft, history, agriculture, diversity and pleasure – while becoming much less prescriptive about how consumers encounter them.

That may mean different formats, occasions, price points, voices and ways of talking about taste. It may mean wine appearing in spaces where it has not traditionally appeared, alongside food, music and culture without demanding that everyone first learn its vocabulary. One of the reasons I detest “minerality” as a descriptor is that it illustrates the problem perfectly: what insiders regard as useful shorthand can sound like nonsense to everyone else.

And it may mean accepting that some of the things enthusiasts consider important simply aren’t important to everyone else. That is not necessarily decline. It may be democratisation.

As we know all too well, vineyards are being pulled out and production is contracting. The difficult work now is not managing abundance but rebuilding demand. We cannot assume that the next generation will inherit wine culture simply because previous generations did. They have more choices, different media habits and different relationships with authority. They also have no obligation to preserve our hierarchies.

So what would I suggest? Use technology to make wine easier to discover and understand, without reducing it to disposable content. Communicate in ways that begin with consumers’ lives rather than wine’s internal vocabulary. Create more opportunities for participation rather than simply more opportunities to consume marketing. And, above all, broaden who gets to shape the category.

For someone like me, there is a final responsibility: to remain useful without assuming that I must remain central. That may be the hardest adjustment of all.

title: Recipe: Tofu, tat soi and shimeji mushroom stir-fry
summary:
Delicious served with steamed rice. Serves 4 Ingredients: 3 tbsp (45ml) sunflower oil 400g tofu, drained and patted dry with absorbent paper 60g shimeji mushrooms, cleaned ¼ cup (60ml) ginger, finely chopped 2 tsp (10ml) sesame seed oil 3 tbsp (45ml) soy sauce 3 tbsp (45ml) sweet chilli sauce squeeze of lemon 200g tat soi, […]

The post Recipe: Tofu, tat soi and shimeji mushroom stir-fry appeared first on winemag.
content:
Serve with Kruger Family Wines Old Vines Cinsault 2017.

Delicious served with steamed rice.

Serves 4

Ingredients:
3 tbsp (45ml) sunflower oil
400g tofu, drained and patted dry with absorbent paper
60g shimeji mushrooms, cleaned
¼ cup (60ml) ginger, finely chopped
2 tsp (10ml) sesame seed oil
3 tbsp (45ml) soy sauce
3 tbsp (45ml) sweet chilli sauce
squeeze of lemon
200g tat soi, washed
15g coriander, chopped
steamed basmati rice, to serve

Method:
Cube tofu into bite size portions and set aside.

Heat sunflower oil in a non-stick pan until hot and gently shallow-fry tofu until golden brown and crispy. Add mushrooms and ginger and stir-fry for further five  minutes. Add sesame oil, soy sauce, sweet chilli sauce and a squeeze of lemon.

Toss in tat soi and remove pan from heat allowing the leaves to wilt. Check seasoning.

Serve with steamed basmati rice and fresh coriander.

Wine pairing:
Light-bodied reds you can chill will work with this dish – think Pinot Noir or new-wave Cinsault.

  • Recipe supplied by Source Food – a Cape Town-based food agency that specializes in experiential marketing. They will create a recipe or meal to communicate your brand’s message.

title: Tim James: Growing older, drinking differently
summary:
We know about old vines and old wines – and their age makes a difference. But what about old wine-drinkers? Does age bring changes, for better or worse, in taste-experiences and preferences? It was a question that the American winewriter and -importer Terry Theise raised in the latest issue of World of Fine Wine, prompted […]

The post Tim James: Growing older, drinking differently appeared first on winemag.
content:
We know about old vines and old wines – and their age makes a difference. But what about old wine-drinkers? Does age bring changes, for better or worse, in taste-experiences and preferences? It was a question that the American winewriter and -importer Terry Theise raised in the latest issue of World of Fine Wine, prompted by his own experience (he didn’t announce it there, but tells me he’s 73). This led to wondering about physical changes that might prompt changes in taste: a supposed reduction in acuity, for example; and he mentioned the presumably hormonal changes in older women – but I guess those in men might also be expected to have consequences.

Theise was surprised, however, to find that most of the small handful of wine-professional friends and colleagues he consulted reported no significant patterns of change in their wine-tastes.

I too am surprised. Easy continuity is not my own experience, whatever the causes of my shifts. Given that I’ve noticeably changed my tastes in various aesthetic areas that are important to me, why not my wine-drinking? These days I seldom read novels, for example, and novel-reading was a defining factor of my life for decades, professional and personal. Overall I now read less than I used to, and it’s usually re-reading rather than anything new, and more often than not it’s non-fiction. My musical tastes have shifted too: it’s still all “classical”, but I can’t easily recall how much I used to love Italian opera (mostly unspeakably silly stuff, I now think, though often kitschly beautiful); and generally I have moved in both temporal directions away from the lushness of nineteenth-century Romanticism.

So, again, why not changes in my tastes in wine as I’ve got older? I’m now 71, having begun a more-or-less serious relationship with wine only in my latter 30s. I don’t think these changes are all obviously ascribable to bodily changes any more than are my shifts in musical and literary tastes … but, yes, maybe some. I have certainly had a general reduction in my taste for sweet foods and drinks in the last decade or two, and that is plausibly related to bodily changes. So my beloved older-style German rieslings often seem too sweet and I would reluctantly admit to, on the whole, preferring drier ones.

When acidity loses its appeal

This is something that Terry Theise strongly notices too. Interestingly (given the high acidity in the best of those sweet rieslings) he also notes a change that he says is more age-typical: a resistance to very high acidity in wines, a character he used to relish. I hadn’t thought of that for myself, but I think it applies. It would help explain why at tastings I seem to object more than my younger colleagues to the “hipster” style of lowish-alcohol, ultra-fresh wines, both white and red, and tend to find them unbalanced and even aggressive in their acidity.

Taking this further, I wonder if this also accounts for my mild turn in the last decade or so away from the red burgundies and local pinot noirs that I previously enjoyed so much more. I’ve returned more , in fact, to an earlier love: cabernet sauvignon-based blends – especially from Bordeaux, especially the dark-fruited, savoury, tannic and “sinister” ones that hark back to pre-1982 times (but seldom South African examples, which I can admire theoretically occasionally, but seldom love, because they are that bit too sunny and friendly, even when not too ripe and powerful). Tannin, then, suits me now more than acidity, it seems.

The pleasures of caring less

As to a decline in acuity – well, I don’t think I’ve ever been acute as a taster, nor have I aspired to become more so, though I realise that this might seem odd for someone who, for example, tasted and rated for the annual Platter’s Guide for two decades. Aiming for the finest, geekiest discrimination has never interested me nearly as much as other aspects of wine (social, historical, cultural, agricultural) – even less now. Decades back, I got through giving up smoking cigarettes without being aware that it made much difference to my palate. Having now joyfully abandoned writing more than the briefest of tasting notes has been an enormous liberation. (I can’t say I frequently read others’ notes either.) It’s very possible that this liberation has itself positively affected the way I enjoy wine in all circumstances: an aura of anxiousness – coming from a sense of responsibility and of my likely inadequacy – doesn’t cloud the pleasure.

There’s much less detail that I’m concerned with these days, Possibly that marks a decline. But I read, just this morning over my toast and marmalade, this apposite line from Montaigne about the comfort he finds in old age, in an essay entitled “All things have their season”:  “that it deadens in me many desires and cares by which life is troubled”, including “care for knowledge”. There’s so much about the vast world of wine that I no longer feel curious about, as I did when I would read the Oxford Companion to Wine cover to cover. That reduction in interest is more of an admission, I suppose, than a boast.

Some changes in my tastes – as reflected in my drinking practices – are clearly not so much so much about ageing as about my growing older in a particular place and time. I’ve had a good few decades chronicling – and drinking – the Cape wine revolution. South African fine white wine is, widely, a miraculously delicate, not to mention delicious, expression of its origins. In response, I now drink nearly as much white wine as red, and that’s a notable shift. As all wine gets more expensive, local and foreign, and I don’t get richer, it suits me well to buy and drink for my pleasure lots of Cape white, and little foreign white apart from sherry and what good German riesling I can afford.

As for the local reds, I prefer the Rhône-style ones, based on syrah or grenache – the whole range of them, including the lighter, fresher ones (but not too light) with no new oak. There’s another change, I think: I now get more pleasure than before from comparatively simple, fairly young wines. I don’t think I’d even want to drink only fine, mature, serious wines, even as an aspiration. Perhaps it’s a sign of greater tolerance.

Something else. I’ve always had a particular passion for fortified wine: sherry, port, madeira. But now, along with drinking some younger, lighter wines, I also go to the opposite extreme and drink a good amount of brandy. I seem to like that kick at the end of the day. My total alcohol consumption has probably declined a little in the last decade, but the proportion of the alcohol intake provided by brandy has increased.

That’s a change in my drinking habits that I am at a total loss to explain. The great revolutionary Leon Trotsky once said that “’Old age is the most unexpected of all things that can happen to a man.” That’s true, I think, and many of the details of the process are just as surprising.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

title: Malu Lambert: The Foundry – 25 Years of Rhône in the Cape
summary:
There is no better way to explore Rhône varieties in South Africa than through The Foundry’s wines, which set a benchmark for a distinctly Cape interpretation. “The Foundry is 25-years-old this year,” says Chris Williams addressing trade and media on the rooftop of the Melting Pot restaurant. The day is vibrantly hot, the surrounding technicolor […]

The post Malu Lambert: The Foundry – 25 Years of Rhône in the Cape appeared first on winemag.
content:
There is no better way to explore Rhône varieties in South Africa than through The Foundry’s wines, which set a benchmark for a distinctly Cape interpretation.

Chris Williams of The Foundry.

“The Foundry is 25-years-old this year,” says Chris Williams addressing trade and media on the rooftop of the Melting Pot restaurant. The day is vibrantly hot, the surrounding technicolor buildings of De Waterkant seem to pulse in its brightness. It’s the new vintage-release and the label’s cold viognier is the perfect counterpoint to the weather.

The Foundry “was born very much out of the impact that the Rhône made on me as a young winemaker travelling in 1994”. Established in an old shed at Joostenberg while Williams was at Meerlust, he left in 2020 to focus on the brand full-time.

“It looks like it was a plan,” he says of the five Rhône-style wines we are about to taste. “It wasn’t. The first vintage [2001] was a mishmash of varieties, but the syrah really stood out.” In 2004, he started co-fermenting syrah with viognier. “I liked the gloss, but not the sweetness and overt florals.” Instead, viognier became The Foundry’s second wine and its first white.

“The range evolved organically.” Part of this is the Cape’s suitability. “There are a lot of similarities with the Rhône,” he says, citing granite soils, a Mediterranean climate, windy summers and cold, wet winters. Crucially, says Williams, “they retain their flavour and acidity.”

White masquerading as red

The Viognier 2024 comes from a vineyard six kilometres from False Bay. At 13 per cent alcohol, it is linear, floral and restrained, with less opulence than typical examples. It’s the only wine made entirely in oak: “Terracotta took away too much of the variety’s perfume.”

We move on to the Grenache Blanc 2022 (Williams says it benefits from bottle age). He points out that few places in the world produce a single varietal. “It’s a very Cape style of wine.” By contrast, some examples he’s tasted in southern France and Spain are “actually quite dull”, where the grape is often used for volume and alcohol.

The grapes come primarily from his own Voor-Paardeberg vineyard with the rest from neighbouring grower Willie Mostert. Williams south-facing block ripens about a week later than Mostert’s sunnier, east-facing vineyard. Each vineyard is split into three cuvées: barrel, stainless steel and terracotta. “What makes it so interesting, both red and white, is the mouthfeel,” he posits. “You get this textural pithiness on the mid-palate after the fruit explosion on entry.”

That component is what draws him to the whites. “They’re thick-skinned because they’ve evolved to deal with the harsh climate of the southern Rhône.” The Foundry whites all have varying degrees of grip balanced by fruit and fresh acidity.

With the Roussanne 2024 now in glass, he points out its gold colour, due to its phenolic character. “I’m careful to balance the natural tannin with roussanne’s generous fruit.” Its skin-to-juice ratio yields just 500 litres per tonne from his Voor-Paardeberg vineyard. “Squish a grape and basically a blob of pulp with four seeds comes out.”

The 2024 is perfumed with incense, turmeric, and Chinese five-spice, offset by savouriness and lemony acidity. Fermented equally in terracotta and barrel, it needs oxygen “to really unlock these exotic flavours”.

“I’ve referred to it, usually after a bottle or two, as red wine in drag.” Roussanne, he adds, has incredible ageing potential, noting that his first vintage was 2010 and “that wine is only now fully mature”. One of his favourite wines, he says, is Château de Beaucastel’s Roussanne Vieilles Vignes, which “is just indestructible”.

Fresh and focused reds

“The inclusion of whole bunch is dependent on the stems,” says Williams, answering a question about the Grenache Noir 2022. “Too green, the wine becomes overtly grassy. Too brown you get a lignified character.”

Heady with roses, the grenache “comes across seductively on the nose, but the palate reminds you that it’s a wine of substance, with this core of tannin.” The key, he says, is picking before overripeness; grenache’s tendency to overcrop and ripen unevenly makes yield and canopy management crucial.

“I don’t like a lot of alcohol; it takes away from the typicity. Freshness and brightness are what I look for.”

The final wine is the Syrah 2022, from Williams’s own Voor-Paardeberg vineyard, planted in 2000. “I like to think of this wine as straddling a tightrope: plenty of freshness, no excess ripeness, quite lithe and muscular. That’s the style the vineyard lends itself to.”

Viognier may not have worked as a blending partner, but Williams has found success with roussanne, which makes up six per cent of the wine. “I discovered too late in life that in Hermitage a lot of growers harvest a bit of roussanne with their syrah.” Unlike viognier, it brings no overt sweetness or perfume, instead it tempers the syrah’s rusticity, glossing its tannins and adding brightness.

While Williams’s unintentional 25-year experiment makes a compelling case for Rhône varieties in the Cape, a conversation with viticulturist Etienne Terblanche after the tasting adds some perspective.

Grenache says Terblanche is the clearest success story. Against the backdrop of an overall decline in vineyard area, grenache noir has grown from around 50 ha in the early 2000s to some 570–580 ha today, while grenache blanc has increased from roughly 20 ha to 170 ha.

Varieties such as marsanne and roussanne grew from a low base but have largely stabilised over the past decade, while viognier, once planted to around 900–1,000 ha, has since roughly halved.

Mourvèdre is also waning. Terblanche believes commercial viability is part of the equation: varieties such as grenache have enough identity to stand alone, while lesser-known grapes primarily associated with blends can be difficult to communicate and sell. Nor he says are these varieties necessarily a simple answer to climate change. While adapted to warm, dry conditions and useful for increasing varietal diversity, many Rhône whites are naturally more about texture than crisp acidity.

The vineyards need to mature too, young plantings of big-berried varieties such as grenache, carignan and cinsault can take time to come into their own.

What do the next 25 years hold for these grapes? While we wait, to borrow from Williams’s favourite writer, Henry David Thoreau: “Live in each season as it passes; breathe the air, drink the drink, taste the fruit…”.

  • Malu Lambert is a freelance wine journalist and wine judge who has written for numerous local and international titles.
